function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you generate the files you need, but I don’t have the ability to run `git clone`, modify a local repository, or push commits back to GitHub from this environment.  
What I can do is:

1. **Generate a Dockerfile** that’s appropriate for a typical Node.js “Hello World” style project (the one you mentioned).  
2. **Create a Kubernetes Deployment + Service YAML** that would deploy that image.  
3. **Provide a GitHub‑Actions workflow** that builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or your registry) whenever you push to `main`.

Below are the exact file contents you can copy into your repository. Once you’ve added them locally, just run the usual `git add`, `git commit`, and `git push` commands.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` gives you a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only the production dependencies listed in `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposes port `3000` – adjust if your app uses a different port.  

If your repo already contains a Dockerfile, replace its contents with the snippet above (or merge the relevant parts).

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

### 2.1 Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change this
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

### 2.2 Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to use:**  
> ```bash
> kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
> kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
> ```

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tag, or service type to suit your environment.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
          cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
          cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add two secrets to your GitHub repo:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token with “write” permissions.  
> * Adjust the image names/tags if you’re using another registry (e.g., GitHub Container Registry, ECR, GCR).

---

## 4. Adding & Pushing the Files

Once you’ve copied the above snippets into your local clone:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Your repo now has a ready‑to‑use Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that automatically builds and publishes the image whenever you push to `main`. If you run into any issues or need further tweaks, let me know!
